newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Farmers pessimistic about Bahia cocoa midcrop.
newsitem.headline: Farmers pessimistic about Bahia cocoa midcrop.

text.p: Bahia cocoa farmers, who had been optimistic about the 1997/8 midcrop before Christmas, said their mood had turned to pessimism following more than a month of dry weather.
"It does not look at all good," said Wallace Setenta, president of the National Cocoa Producers' Council.
"The last decent rain fell on the 14th and 15th of December. Since then we've hardly seen a drop."
Setenta said the last midcrop, harvested from May to September, had produced around 1.5 million 60-kilo bags but he feared that this year's would be smaller.

Heavy rains last week caused serious flooding in the southeastern states of Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espirito Santo. But Bahia, which lies immediately to the north, had remained mainly dry, Setenta said.
"The rain got as far as Minas and stopped there," Setenta said.
More bad news for beleagured farmers was that internal prices, which had been at around 21 Real per 15-kilo arroba until the end of last year, had stuck at around 17 Real for the second week running.
Setenta said the only good news for producers was they were on the point of receiving the second lot of government credits to help them fight witch's broom disease.
The disease has been responsible for the drop in local production over the last five years and the consequent crisis which has afflicted the region.
He said farmers were hoping to start receiving the credits, worth a total of around 120 million Real, this month.
But he said the money should have been distributed in June and July of last year to enable farmers to carry out husbandry for the main crop which is currently being harvested.
"The money is not being distributed in line with the agricultural calender," he said.
He said the CNPC had contacted the government proposing that the whole programme, in which two more lots of credits are due to be handed out, be revampted.
The producers' main proposals are for the money to be handed out at the time when farmers are preparing for the next crop and for less bureacracy.
He said that farmers at present have to produce a variety of documents before their applications for loans are considered.
